**The X-33's central problem did not go away when the programme did, and the modern literature on it is larger and more capable than the literature the programme had.**
This section surveys that work. The organising principle is the chain of the article's argument, so the
subsections run from the tank outward.

### Composite Cryogenic Tanks Since the X-33

**This field descends directly from the article's subject, and it is active.** The problems are the
ones the failure investigation named, and the modern work addresses them directly.
[Bae et al. 2025][research_bae_jin_2025] treats permeation barrier layers, [Timmerman et al. 2002][research_timmerman_hayes_2002] and
[Nobelen et al. 2003][research_nobelen_hayes_2003] treat nanomodified and toughened resin systems, [Paul et al. 2021][research_paul_andrea_2021] treats
microcrack-resistant matrices for out-of-autoclave processing, and [Jackson et al. 2015][research_jacksonjustinr_vickersjohn_2015] reports
out-of-autoclave tanks 2.4 and 5.5 metres across. The cluster on composite cryogenic tanks and pressure
vessels below holds the tanks themselves.

### Microcracking and Permeability

**The mechanism this article derives from thermal expansion mismatch is now a subject in its own right**,
with a literature on crack density evolution under thermomechanical cycling, as in [McManus 1994][research_mcmanushughl_1994] and
[Shimokawa et al. 2002][research_shimokawa_katoh_2002], on the relationship between crack density and gas transport, which [Yokozeki et al. 2003][research_yokozeki_aoki_2003],
[Yokozeki et al. 2004][research_yokozeki_aoki_2004] and [Roy et al. 2004][research_roy_utturkar_2004] examine, and on resin systems formulated to resist cryogenic
microcracking, among them [Timmerman et al. 2002][research_timmerman_hayes_2002] and [Paul et al. 2021][research_paul_andrea_2021]. All of it appears below under
microcracking, permeation and leakage of laminates.

### Sandwich Structures, Cores and Debonding

**The failure was a facesheet-to-core separation, and sandwich debonding now has a substantial literature**,
including detection methods the programme did not have, among them guided Lamb waves in [Sikdar and Ostachowicz 2018][research_sikdar_ostachowicz_2018] and
[Yu et al. 2018][research_yu_tian_2018] and laser ultrasonics in [Sen et al. 2020][research_sen_saito_2020]. Below, they are listed under sandwich
structures, honeycomb cores and the face-to-core bond.

### Buckling, and a Factor of 1968 That Is Still Being Argued About

**The identity derived above places the cost of conformality outside membrane mechanics, so the answer must lie in the buckling and stability literature.**
That literature also holds the article's least certain assumption, and that assumption turns out to be the
subject of a sustained modern effort.

**The knockdown factor swept in the sizing section comes from a monograph published in 1968.** Those factors
are lower-bound envelopes drawn under test data collected across the preceding decades, and they are
deliberately conservative, because a buckling allowable that is optimistic destroys vehicles.
**Conservatism in a buckling allowable is paid directly in structural mass**, so the modern work aims to
replace an empirical lower bound with analysis that uses measured or modelled imperfections and returns a
factor the structure has earned.

**What that conservatism is worth on this vehicle depends entirely on whether the wall is a sandwich, and the difference between the two answers is a factor of 38.1.**
Moving the knockdown from 0.2 to 0.5 takes the buckling-equivalent thickness from 3.660 millimetres to
2.315. On the composite sandwich, where bending stiffness is bought with core separation rather than with
material, the core needed for stiffness parity falls from 3.00 millimetres to 1.51 and the saving across
both tanks is

$$\left(m_{0.2} - m_{0.5}\right) S = 103 \ \text{lb}$$

**On a metal monocoque of the same geometry, where the thickness is the stiffness, the same change in the same factor saves**

$$\left(\rho_{Al} t_{0.2} - \rho_{Al} t_{0.5}\right) S = 3{,}932 \ \text{lb}$$

**which is 5.24 percent of the vehicle's burnout mass.** Set against the burnout-mass growth that cost the Mach 15
objective, taken from the two ends of the table in the section headed The Speed Objective as a
Weight Report,

$$m_f - m_f^{\ast} = 75{,}000 - 66{,}969 = 8{,}031 \ \text{lb} , \qquad 75{,}000 - 68{,}489 = 6{,}511 \ \text{lb} ,$$

$$\frac{3{,}932}{8{,}413} = 0.467 , \qquad \frac{3{,}932}{6{,}824} = 0.576 ,$$

**the monocoque saving is between 49.0 and 60.4 percent of that weight growth of 6,511 to 8,031 pounds.**

**So a sandwich is very nearly insulated from the conservatism of a buckling allowable and a metal monocoque is not.**
That gives a second and independent reason the architecture was right, one not usually given
for it. It also holds beyond the one point computed here, since a sandwich at stiffness
parity is lighter than the metal monocoque it replaces at every knockdown between one twentieth and one,
tested across twenty thousand values.

**An uncomfortable corollary follows.** A programme that needed mass, and that reduced its
speed objective because it could not find any, was sizing structure against a factor known to be
conservative and known to be improvable.
**Whether better factors were available to it in the 1990s is not something this article can establish**,
and the modern literature is evidence that the problem was open rather than evidence that the answer
existed. That literature includes the agency's own programme to develop new shell buckling design
factors in [Hilburger 2012][research_hilburgermarkw_2012], the reassessment of knockdowns in [Gerasimidis et al. 2018][research_gerasimidis_virot_2018] and the review in [Wang et al. 2022f][research_wang_hao_2022], and it fills the cluster
on shell buckling, knockdown factors and imperfection sensitivity below.

### Metallic Tanks, Alloys and Welding

**The comparison the programme was forced into is a live subject**, covering aluminium-lithium alloys such as
the 2195 gores of [Volz 2015][research_volzmartin_2015], the friction stir welding of tank structure studied by [Chen and Russell 2012][research_chen_russell_2012] and
[Wang et al. 2018b][research_wang_zhao_2018], and the hydrogen compatibility of metals treated in [Cavaliere 2025c][research_cavaliere_2025]. The cluster on metallic
tanks, aluminium-lithium alloys, welding and hydrogen embrittlement below collects them.

### Cryogenic Insulation and Boil-Off

**The insulation system, the purge cavity and the sealed core are one arrangement**, and modern work on
cryogenic insulation and boil-off continues the part of it the article treats least, from launch-vehicle foam in [Fesmire et al. 2011][research_fesmireje_cofmanbe_2011] to zero boil-off storage in [Hastings et al. 2001][research_hastings_plachta_2001].
Its records are listed below under cryogenic insulation, boil-off and propellant management.

### Cryogenic Hydrogen Beyond Launch Vehicles

**This is the subsection that would have surprised the programme.** The structural problem of holding liquid
hydrogen in a lightweight conformal vessel is now an aviation problem for [Bagarello 2024][research_bagarello_2024], a maritime one
for [Çetinkaya et al. 2026][research_cetinkaya_korkmaz_2026] and a rail one for [Kang et al. 2022][research_kang_yun_2022], driven by decarbonisation rather
than by launch. That work is gathered in the cluster on liquid hydrogen storage for aircraft, ships and road
vehicles below.
**The X-33's question is being asked again by people who have never heard of it**, and the constraints are
similar enough that the literatures are converging.

### The Aerospike Returned Through Manufacture Rather Than Through Aerodynamics

**The engine architecture that worked has continued to attract analysis**, largely computational, and the
modern treatments address the base-flow behaviour this article declines to attempt.

**But the interesting change is not in the aerodynamics.** An annular or linear plug is a great many small
thrust chambers and a contoured ramp, and what made it expensive in the 1990s was building that.
**Additive manufacturing removes most of the reason it was expensive**, which is why the architecture has
reappeared in small engines rather than in large ones, as in [Peugeot et al. 2014][research_peugeotjohn_garciachance_2014] and
[Whitmore and Armstrong 2019][research_whitmore_armstrong_2019], where the part count is lower and the manufacturing saving is proportionally larger. The
aerospike and plug nozzle records below carry that literature.

**The tank's afterlife was of a different kind.** The composite cryotank came back because the
problem was understood better. The aerospike came back because the machine tools changed.

### Reusability and the Economics That Actually Changed

**The goal the programme was chartered to pursue was achieved by other means, and the literature on launch economics and reusability documents that outcome.**
The cost of reusability was argued in [Keith 1995][research_keith_1995] before the X-33 award, and a fully reusable super-heavy system
is costed in [Harris et al. 2022][research_harris_ledford_2022]. The records under reusability, launch cost
and operations below contain it.

### Computation, Surrogates and Uncertainty

**A great deal of what the programme had to settle by building could now be examined by computation**, and
the fair question, raised in Where the Framing Breaks Down, is whether the unmodelled
failure mode would have been any more visible to a modern analysis than to a period one. Surrogate and
reduced-order methods of the kind in [Brevault et al. 2019][research_brevault_balesdent_2019] and [Chen et al. 2015b][research_chen_liu_2015], and uncertainty quantification of
the kind in [Brevault and Balesdent 2021][research_brevault_balesdent_2021], are applied to whole vehicles, and the structural part of that literature
makes up the cluster on computation, optimisation and uncertainty in structural design below.

### Sandwich structures, honeycomb cores and the face-to-core bond

**The wall the conformal tank required.** Sandwich mechanics, honeycomb and foam cores, face wrinkling and core failure, and the face-to-core bond with its fracture, debonding and detection.

**A cancelled programme stops generating literature under its own name.** In the survey, 78 titles carry the X-33 designation, 71 of them predate 2002, and the latest is dated 2017. Those of 2002 and later are reports completed after cancellation and retrospective accounts, among them [Ehrlich 2009][research_ehrlich_2009] on why the programme gave single-stage-to-orbit a bad name and [McCurdy 2017][research_mccurdy_2017] on its public-private partnership. This is the documentary consequence of cancellation and the mirror image of the finding in the previous article, where a losing competitor stopped generating literature the moment it lost.

## Where the Framing Breaks Down

### The Single Point of Failure Is a Story, Not an Explanation

**The most common account of the X-33 is that a tank failed and a programme died, and this article has spent considerable effort arguing against that reading while relying on the same tank.**
The distinction needs care.

**The tank did not fail because it was a tank. It failed because of a chain.** The vehicle must land
horizontally, so it is a lifting body, so its cross-section is not circular, so the tank must be conformal,
so it must be lobed, so its walls carry bending, so they are sandwiches, so they have cores, and the core is
the thing that killed it. **Change any link and the failure mode changes.**

**But the chain is an explanation of the mechanism and not of the cancellation**, and conflating the two is
the trap. The arithmetic of What the Data Changed shows that the programme had a mass problem that the tank failure
did not create and that fixing the tank would not have solved.

### The Counterfactual That Does Not Work

**Suppose the tank had not failed.** The composite tanks would have flown, the vehicle would have made some
number of suborbital flights, and the programme would have declared its technologies demonstrated.
**And VentureStar's hydrogen tanks would still have been 41 percent of its structural allowance**, by the
earlier calculation of the verdict, because that number comes from the tank's mass,
which was known.

**So the failure did not decide anything that the mass had not already decided.** What the failure did was
make the decision unavoidable and public.
**A programme can carry an unfavourable number for years. It cannot carry a photograph of a tank in pieces.**

### Where This Article's Own Framing Is Weakest

**The keystone chosen here is the mass fraction and the tank, and a reader could reasonably choose differently.**
A programme-management reading, in which the cooperative agreement structure and the absence of realistic
cost and risk planning are the subject, is defensible and is
[the reading the Government Accountability Office took when it examined the two cancelled programmes together][ref_gao_x33x34].
**That reading explains the cancellation better than this one does and explains the engineering worse.**

**A second weakness is the treatment of the aerospike.** This article says the engine worked and moves on. A
propulsion-centred treatment would ask what altitude compensation is worth over a real trajectory rather
than at two points, and would have to confront the base-flow behaviour of a truncated plug, the hard
part of the architecture, which this article does not attempt.

**A third is that the tank efficiency figure carries the whole verdict.** It rests on a reported tank mass
of 4,600 pounds and a reported capacity of 29,000 gallons. If either is wrong the verdict moves
proportionally. The consistency check below is the only defence available, and a weak one.

### The Numbers That Hold Each Other Up

**Three figures published separately, and never on the same page, can be checked against one another.** The
tank capacity, the propellant load and the engine mixture ratio imply a fill fraction. The hydrogen load
implied by 210,000 pounds of propellant at a mixture ratio of 5.5 is 14,655 kilograms, which occupies 206.85
cubic metres, against a total tank capacity of 219.55, so

$$\frac{206.85}{219.55} = 0.942$$

**The implied fill is 94.2 percent**, consistent with what a cryogenic tank carries once ullage is allowed
for.

**Had the fill come out above unity, or below three quarters, one of the three published numbers would have been wrong.**
It did not, so the tank mass figure that carries the verdict sits inside a set of numbers that are mutually
consistent. **That is corroboration and not proof, and the article states it as corroboration.**

## The Source Base

**The research survey holds 5,323 research records drawn from Crossref, the NASA Technical Reports Server and the Defense Technical Information Center**, of which 937 are report primaries, being 17.6 percent, by the identifier rule set out under The Definition of Primary. **The median publication year is 2010.** Of the 5,289 dated records, 2,132 were published through 2001, when the programme was cancelled, being 40.4 percent, 2,484 were published in 2015 or later, being 47.0 percent, and 1,291 in 2022 or later, being 24.4 percent.

### The Definition of Primary

**Primacy is a property of the document, and this survey derives it from the identifier.** A record is a report primary when its address is on the NASA Technical Reports Server or it carries a digital object identifier under the 10.21236 prefix, which Crossref registers for Defense Technical Information Center reports. **The rule does not reach the conference papers in which much of the programme's own engineering was published**, such as the American Institute of Aeronautics and Astronautics papers on the X-33, so 17.6 percent is a lower bound on how much of the survey is first-hand.

**A primary source is one contemporary with the work, and for this article the work has an unusually clean boundary.**
The X-33 programme ran from the Phase II award on 2 July 1996 to cancellation in early 2001, and the reports
server holds the programme's own documents from that window in quantity.
**That is the opposite of the previous article's situation and the contrast is measurable.** The X-32 article
finds a single title carrying that designation in its survey.
**Of the 5,323 research records this article cites, 78 carry the X-33 designation in their titles**,
because the vehicle's own documentation was never the thin part.

**The reason is institutional rather than accidental.** A defence competitor is documented by its
manufacturer and its customer, and a National Aeronautics and Space Administration cooperative agreement is
documented by a research agency that publishes.
**The designation is the same in both cases and the documentary consequence is not.**

### The Technology Base Predates the Programme

**A second primary base sits earlier.** The composite structures work, the sandwich mechanics, the
lifting-body aerodynamics and the plug nozzle analysis were largely done in the 1960s through the 1980s. A
1970s report on plug nozzle base pressure is therefore a primary source for this article's propulsion
section in a way that a 2020 computational study is not, and the design-space studies of the period, such as
[Hunt's single-stage-to-orbit design matrix][book_airbreathing_rocket_single_stage_to_orbi], belong to the
same window.

### The Failure Investigation

**The investigation itself is thinly represented in the retrievable record and this is a genuine gap.** The
summary findings are available in secondary and review form and are cited here as such.
**The primary investigation documentation is largely presentation material, and the copies that are retrievable are scanned images from which no text can be extracted.**
That limitation is stated rather than written around.

### The Weakest Link in the Source Chain

**The claim that the composite tank came out heavier than an aluminium tank of the same shape rests on secondary sources**,
and the article flags it at the point of use as well as here. It is consistent with the derivation and with
the reported role of the joints,
**but consistency with a derivation is not evidence, and a result that agrees with one's own analysis deserves more scepticism rather than less.**

### Thin Subjects

**Five subjects that this article's derivations depend on have thin literatures.** Each count below is the number of research records in this survey whose title carries at least one of the listed terms, with a hyphen read as a space. Where a row joins two groups of terms with the word together, a title must carry a term from each group.

| Subject | Title terms counted | Records |
|---|---|---|
| the minimum gauge of a facesheet | minimum gauge, minimum gage | 1 |
| flatwise tension of the face-to-core bond | flatwise tensile, flatwise tension | 6 |
| cryopumping into a cold structure | cryopumping, cryopump, cryopumped | 3 |
| multi-lobe and conformal tanks | multi lobe, multilobe, lobed, conformal together with tank, tanks | 11 |
| weight growth during development | weight growth, mass growth | 2 |

**Minimum gauge is a constraint of manufacture with almost no literature under its own name.** One title names it, [McQuigg et al. 2011][research_mcquigg_kapania_2011], on honeycomb panels with minimum-gage glass-fibre facesheets in compression, so the argument that minimum gauge governs the facesheet rests on the arithmetic above rather than on a body of measurement.

**The test of the bond that failed is standard, and its behaviour against liquid hydrogen is not a subject in its own right.** Six titles name flatwise tension, 5 of them dated 2020 or later, among them the stress analysis of the test specimen in [Scott and Pereira 1993][research_scott_pereira_1993], and none names a cryogenic temperature.

**The mechanism that pressurised the core is named in three titles.** Cryopumping is otherwise a word of vacuum engineering, and of the three only [Johnson et al. 2003b][research_theodorefjohnson_eriksweiser_2003] concerns the insulation of a reusable launch vehicle tank.

**The conformal tank has a small literature that is growing again for aircraft.** Of the eleven titles, 3 date from 1998 to 2000 and 5 from 2023 onward, 2 of those for liquid-hydrogen aircraft, and one, [Ko 2004a][research_kowilliaml_2004], analyses the debonding stresses of a pressurised lobed sandwich-walled cryogenic tank, which is the wall this article sizes.

**Weight growth, which cost the programme its Mach 15 objective, is named in two titles**, two versions of one study in [Dissel et al. 2005][research_dissel_kothari_2005] and [Dissel et al. 2007][research_dissel_kothari_2007], so the weight growth inversion stands on the article's derivation from the published speed objectives rather than on a published analysis of growth.

### What the Survey Admits

**A record is admitted only when a person reading its title finds it on this article's subject.** Many words this subject depends on also name something else, and a record that shares only such a word is excluded. Tank also names battle tanks and artillery, permeability also names petroleum reservoirs, coal seams, underground gas storage and the resin flow through fibre preforms, buckling also names the lateral buckling of subsea pipelines, and cryogenic insulation also names the electrical insulation of cryogenic cables and magnets. Cryopumping also names the vacuum pumps of space simulation chambers, molecular beam apparatus and fusion beam injectors, which share the physics of condensation and none of the subject. A plug nozzle is also the exhaust plug of a turbojet and a subject of jet noise, an aerospike is also a drag-reducing spike on a hypersonic body, lithium-aluminium is also a target alloy for tritium production, debonding and laminates also belong to solid propellant grains, spray foam insulation is also a building material, and the propellant tanks of satellites hold storable propellants rather than cryogens. Bond strength also names the bonding of dental adhesives, and readiness also names organisational readiness assessments. Records on concrete and civil engineering, road and rail vehicles other than their hydrogen storage, markets and pricing, nuclear power plants, ordnance and military organisation, medicine and consumer technology share words with this subject in the same way and are excluded as well. Planetary ascent, entry and landing, nuclear and electric propulsion, and metal matrix and ceramic matrix composites outside thermal protection are excluded as distant from an Earth-to-orbit reusable launcher with a polymer composite tank. Correction, erratum, retraction and withdrawal notices, peer-review records, standards and material specifications, patents, conference volumes and journal front matter are excluded, because a survey counts research works and those are parts of works, editorial events or documents of another kind. Twin deposits of one document under more than one identifier are counted once.

**A record whose only link to this subject is launch or aeronautics in general is excluded too**, and so is one whose subject belongs to a class of vehicle or a system the argument never uses. Expendable and small-satellite launchers and their programmes, the orbital missions of upper stages, missiles, hypersonic glide weapons, airbreathing cruise vehicles, sounding rockets and drones are such classes. Ascent guidance laws, inertial and satellite navigation and the attitude control of expendable launchers are excluded, and so are launcher avionics, acoustics, pogo, separation systems and reliability models, solid, hybrid, in-space and low-thrust propulsion, and studies of engine combustion, injection, cooling and nozzle physics that bear on none of reuse, vehicle sizing and the plug nozzle. Hydrogen aircraft studies whose titles do not concern the tank are excluded from the literature on hydrogen storage. Monitoring, inspection and uncertainty methods whose titles name no structure of the kind this article sizes are excluded as well. A method or phenomenon the argument relies on is admitted whatever the vehicle, so the guidance and control of reusable and reentry vehicles, the return and landing of reusable boosters, the thermal protection of any hypersonic vehicle and the flow separation of any rocket nozzle are kept.

**Reviews of books, reference and definition entries and notices are not admitted, and a document deposited twice is admitted once.** An authored encyclopedia article of more than two pages and a chapter of a textbook are research works and are kept, and where one document is held twice the journal or report version is the one admitted.

**Some records of doubtful relevance are kept.** Hydrogen embrittlement of steels and nickel alloys in oil, gas, subsea and pipeline service is kept, because the hydrogen compatibility of metals is the same question. The buckling of steel storage tanks and offshore shells is kept, because the knockdown problem is the same. Ascent trajectory optimisation for expendable launchers is kept, because it bears on the velocity budget the sizing takes as its input. Hydrogen storage for aircraft, ships and road vehicles is kept as the literature this subject now belongs to, and a reader may weigh each accordingly. **No cluster is a residual.** Every record sits in the cluster its title names, and the two general structural clusters, on computation in structural design and on shells, plates and pressure structures, hold the records of those literatures whose titles address structures of the kind this article sizes.

**Every research title has been read for relevance, so the off-topic share that remains is a matter of reading judgement.** A reading of titles cannot show that a work is relevant in substance, so this is a statement about titles only.

## Epistemic State

### Historical Fact

The Phase II cooperative agreement was awarded to Lockheed Martin on 2 July 1996. The composite liquid
hydrogen tank failed on 3 November 1999 at Marshall Space Flight Center, after its test programme had been
completed successfully and the tank drained, with the separation occurring approximately fifteen minutes
later. The investigation ran from mid-November 1999 to early February 2000 and reported a combination of
causes including microcracking with hydrogen infiltration, cryopumping of the nitrogen purge, elevated core
pressures, reduced bondline strength and toughness, and manufacturing flaws. The liquid oxygen tank was
aluminium, chosen under a contractual option for schedule reasons. The flight speed objective was reduced
from Mach 15 to Mach 13.8 during detailed design because projected weight exceeded requirements. The
programme was cancelled in the early months of 2001 without a flight. The Government Accountability Office
reported the agency contribution to the agreement at 912.4 million dollars and the industry contribution at
an estimated 286.6 million as of 1999.

### Engineering Analysis

The propellant mass fraction of 0.8898 required for orbit, and the 86.4 to 90.3 percent bracket across the
sensitivity sweep, are this article's derivation from the rocket equation under stated assumptions about
velocity requirement and specific impulse. The hydrogen volume share of 74.6 percent, the bulk density
figures and the ratio of 2.983 are arithmetic on published densities, the engine mixture ratio of 5.5, and
an assumed kerosene mixture ratio of 2.56. The
membrane vessel mass law with shape factors of three halves and two is standard and is re-derived here. The
ideal tank fractions of 2.852 and 0.342 percent depend on assumed material allowables and are swept. The web
tension result, that it equals pressure times centre separation, is derived here and its limiting cases
check.
**The identity that the membrane mass per unit enclosed volume of a lobed section equals that of a cylinder exactly is derived here and verified to machine precision on the X-33 geometry against numerically obtained area and arc length rather than closed forms.**
The cryopumping fill fractions and the constant-volume warming pressure are ideal gas arithmetic. The
thermal mismatch strain of 1.306 percent and its ratio of 2.18 to the transverse failure strain rest on
assumed ply properties which are typical rather than measured. The nozzle comparison is ideal
one-dimensional flow and is checked against the sonic condition. The weight growth inversion of 9.5 to 12.0
percent is derived from the published speed objectives at an assumed cutoff altitude of 180,000 feet and is
checked forward. The conversion from Mach number to velocity at that altitude is an assumption, and a cutoff at
250,000 feet would give 8.4 to 10.6 percent.

### Inference

**That the failure mechanism was thermodynamically forced rather than a workmanship defect is an inference, and it rests on the thermal mismatch arithmetic alone.**
The position of manufacturing flaws within the investigation's list of five causes is not evidence either
way,
**because the published summaries order those five differently and a list of contributing causes is not a ranking.**
The arithmetic is the whole of the support. The inference is strong, but the investigation did not
state it.

**That the cancellation was decided by mass rather than by the tank failure is an inference**, and the
Government Accountability Office's programme-management reading is a competing account that the record
supports at least as well.

**That the linear scale ratio of 1.972 corroborates the half-scale description** is an inference from two
masses under a cube law, and a vehicle is not a geometrically similar object.

### What the Record Does Not Settle

**Whether VentureStar's tanks could have reached the required efficiency is not settled by anything here.**
This article shows that a factor between 1.6 and 4.1 was needed depending on the budget allowed, and that no
such factor had been demonstrated. It does not show that the factor was unreachable.

**Whether the programme would have been cancelled without the tank failure is not settled**, and the
counterfactual is unanswerable in principle.

**The reported relative weights of the composite and aluminium-lithium tanks are not settled** by any
primary source this article could retrieve.

**The precise cancellation date is given variously as February and as March 2001** in the sources consulted,
and the article says early 2001 rather than choosing.

## Out of Scope

The base-flow and plume behaviour of a truncated plug nozzle, the difficult part of the
aerospike architecture. The detailed aerothermodynamics of the lifting-body shape. The guidance and control
design in any depth. The X-34, which was cancelled alongside the X-33 and which this series treats
separately. The Space Launch Initiative that followed. The commercial and financial case for VentureStar,
including the market forecasts that underwrote it. The politics of the cancellation decision.

## Conclusion

**The X-33 was cancelled because its demonstration worked.**

That is neither a paradox nor a defence of the programme. A technology demonstrator exists to find out
whether a technology will do what a vehicle needs.
**The X-33's tank was built, was tested, and returned an answer**, and the answer was legible in two
independent ways. It failed in a manner that showed the linerless composite sandwich cryotank of that
generation was not ready, and, separately and more damningly,
**it weighed 26.83 percent of the hydrogen it held, which extrapolates to 41.0 percent of VentureStar's entire structural allowance.**
The second number needed no failure to be true.

**The chain that produced the failure is the article's main technical contribution and it runs one way.**
Land on a runway, and the vehicle is a lifting body. Make it a lifting body, and the tank must be conformal.
Make it conformal, and it must be lobed. Lobe it, and the walls carry bending. Carry bending, and the wall
is a sandwich. Build a sandwich, and there is a core, and the core is a sealed void against liquid hydrogen
at twenty kelvin. **Every link is forced by the one before it.**

**And the membrane model, the natural first choice of a designer, finds the whole chain free.** The
identity derived here is exact. The web costs precisely what the volume it encloses is worth, at every
radius and every separation.
**A cost model that returns zero for a decision that turned out to be expensive is not a small problem, and locating the missing terms, namely bending, buckling, minimum gauge and joints, is the practical lesson.**

**Pricing those terms turned up a defence of the architecture that is not the one usually offered.**
Buckling governs the wall, a sandwich is the affordable answer to buckling, and a sandwich buys its
stiffness from separation rather than from material.
**One consequence is that a sandwich is very nearly indifferent to how conservative the buckling allowable is, and a metal monocoque is not.**
Improving a 1968 knockdown factor from 0.2 to 0.5 is worth 103 pounds on these tanks as built and 3,932 on a
metal monocoque of the same geometry,
**the second figure being roughly half the weight growth that cost the programme its Mach 15 objective.**
The architecture that brought the sealed core also bought immunity from an allowance nobody could tighten.

**Set beside the previous article the pair is instructive.** The [X-32][related_post_a329_boeing_x32] was
flown against a rival and could not answer its question, because neither demonstrator was the aircraft being
bought. The X-33 never flew and could answer its question, because the quantity that mattered was
scale-invariant and could be weighed on the ground.
**A vehicle that never left the ground produced a cleaner result than one that flew one hundred and forty-four times**,
and the lesson concerns experimental design rather than either aeroplane.

**The designation went to a vehicle that was never finished, and the programme still found something out.**
This series has now met a designation marking an absence of demand in the
[X-27][related_post_a324_lockheed_x27], an absence of knowledge in the
[X-30][related_post_a327_rockwell_x30], and, here, **the presence of an answer nobody wanted.**

"SCALING METHODOLOGY FOR BUCKLING OF COMPOSITE CONICAL SHELLS IN AXIAL COMPRESSIONConical Shells Are Commonly Used as Structural Components for Launch Vehicles. the Axial Compression Experienced during Launch Is One of the Sizing Load Cases, Because It Can Lead to Loss of Structural Stability. Because Experimentally Testing These Full-Scale Structures Is Cumbersome and Expensive, It Is Expedient to Understand How Reduced-Scale Shells Can Be Designed Such That Their Buckling Behavior Is Representative of the Full-Scale Shell Behavior. an Analytical, Sequential Scaling Methodology Is Developed Based on the Nondimensional Governing Equations for Composite Conical Shells with a Symmetric, Balanced Layup and Negligible Flexural Anisotropy. Linear and Nonlinear Finite Element Analyses Characterizing the Buckling Behavior of the Different Size Shells Yielded Comparable Results in Terms of Buckling Load, Meridional Displacement, and Buckling Mode. the Inclusion of Geometric Imperfections Affects the Prediction Accuracy, but Not to the Extent That the Methodology Is No Longer Valid."
